claims.text: Ethanol oxidation involves a 12-electron and 12-proton transfer process.
Electrochemical potential cycling induces dynamic, reversible oxidation-state shifts in the platinum-group catalyst.
The reversible oxidation-state shifts govern the catalyst's superior ethanol-oxidation performance.
High potentials generate transient oxidized platinum species such as Pt-OH.
Surface oxide or hydroxide intermediates lower activation barriers for multi-electron and multi-proton ethanol-oxidation steps.
Returning to a lower potential restores the active sites to a reduced metallic state.
Periodic restoration of the metallic state preserves catalyst structural integrity and long-term durability.
The initial platinum-group catalyst can be maintained at a stable equilibrium predominantly in its reduced metallic state.
Potential cycling will produce reversible XAS absorption-edge shifts corresponding to oxidation and reduction of the platinum-group sites.
XAS can detect potential-dependent changes in the oxidation state and coordination environment of the active sites.
Potential cycling will enhance ethanol-conversion rates relative to a constant-potential baseline.
Potential cycling will improve selectivity toward complete ethanol-oxidation products relative to a constant-potential baseline.
Moderate potential cycling produces reversible rather than irreversible catalyst redox changes.
Excessively high potentials cause irreversible oxidation of the catalyst.
Potentials that are too low fail to generate the proposed active oxide species.
The exact potential window needed to balance oxidized-species formation and catalyst regeneration is unknown.
The specific oxide or hydroxide species responsible for enhanced activity is unknown.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats failure to observe reversible oxidation-state transitions as falsifying, whereas the boundary states that such a failure is expected when the selected potentials are too low or too high. Because the potential window is not specified, absence of the transition is not by itself decisive.
